opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth separating two questions: whether someone *will* build a cluster of that scale, and whether that's what's *required* for the kind of progress people are talking about.

On the first, I wouldn't bet against it. The scaling trends of the last several years have been remarkably consistent, and there's enormous capital flowing in. If the returns keep coming, someone will keep pushing. Extrapolating the curves isn't crazy; it's what has worked so far.

But I'm more skeptical about the framing that sheer compute is *the* bottleneck. Much of the progress we've seen comes from scaling models trained on human-generated data, and that data is finite. At some point you run into the question of where new, genuinely novel information comes from. You can throw ten times more compute at the same internet, but you won't necessarily get ten times more interesting capabilities.

That's why I'm so interested in open-endedness: systems that generate their own learning opportunities, their own problems, their own data, the way evolution or science keeps producing novelty without a fixed dataset. In that world compute still matters hugely, because these self-improvement loops are expensive. But how you spend it matters as much as how much you have. A smarter algorithm for generating the right curriculum, or for deciding what's interesting to explore next, can be worth orders of magnitude of brute force.

So my honest assessment is: trillion-dollar clusters may well happen, and they'll probably buy real capabilities. But I don't think they're a sufficient condition for something like general, open-ended intelligence, and I'm not even fully convinced they're necessary. I'd want to see as much investment in the algorithmic ideas as in the data centers. Historically, that's often where the surprising jumps come from.

r001.rationale: The response says recent scaling trends have been consistent and that extrapolating the curves is plausible, but it does not characterize those trends as exponential growth.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose that progress follows a succession of sigmoid curves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating two things there. One is the question of whether people will actually build clusters at that scale, and the other is whether that's what's required to get to very capable AI. On the first question, honestly, given the amount of capital flowing in and the incentives of the big labs and the hyperscalers, I wouldn't be surprised if someone does it. If you look at the trajectory from the early GPT models to where we are now, the compute spend has gone up by orders of magnitude, and the scaling laws have held up remarkably well. So from a purely empirical standpoint, there's a strong argument that more compute keeps paying off, and people will keep paying for it.

But I'm a bit more skeptical that it's required, and this is where my own research background shapes how I think about it. A lot of my work has been on open-endedness, on systems that generate their own curriculum, their own challenges, and improve from that. And what I keep coming back to is that the most important thing isn't just the raw amount of compute, it's what you do with it. If you think about how humans learn, we're not trained on the entire internet. We learn from a relatively small amount of experience, but that experience is incredibly well targeted. Children are curious, they seek out exactly the things that are at the edge of what they can already do. So I think there's a huge amount of headroom in using compute more intelligently rather than just using more of it.

There's also a practical point. Pre-training on human-generated data is going to hit a wall, because we're running out of high-quality text. So a trillion-dollar cluster trained the way we train models today runs into diminishing returns on the data side regardless. The interesting question is where you point that compute instead. I think a lot of it will shift towards things like search at inference time, towards self-play and synthetic environments, towards models generating and verifying their own training signal. And those regimes have very different economics. Some of them might actually be more compute-hungry, not less, because you're exploring rather than imitating.

So my honest assessment is that these predictions are probably right about the direction and maybe even the scale of investment, but I think they overstate the inevitability. I'd rather bet on algorithmic progress and better learning paradigms than on brute force alone. Historically, if you look at what's actually delivered the big jumps, it's been a combination of both, and the algorithmic side tends to get underestimated in these conversations because it's harder to put a dollar figure on it.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe technological progress as a succession of sigmoid curves or contrast that pattern with one indefinitely continuing exponential curve.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be quite humble about predictions like that. There’s a difference between saying that someone might build a trillion-dollar compute cluster and saying that progress in AI will require one. The latter is a much stronger claim.

Compute has clearly been a powerful driver of progress, and there are good reasons to keep investing in it. But projecting a spending curve forward doesn’t tell you what algorithmic improvements we’ll discover, how efficiently we’ll use that compute, or where the next bottleneck will be.

So I wouldn’t dismiss the possibility, but I also wouldn’t treat it as inevitable. The interesting question is what additional capability that investment buys you—and whether there are more efficient ways to get there.

r001.rationale: It cautions against projecting a spending curve forward, but does not describe the trillion-dollar prediction as an extrapolation of current exponential growth trends.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty and possible algorithmic improvements, but does not propose successive sigmoid curves instead of one continuing exponential curve.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be cautious about putting a precise number or timeline on it. There are really two questions: whether someone will build a trillion-dollar compute cluster, and whether that much compute will be necessary to make progress. Those aren’t the same thing.

We’ve seen that scaling compute can produce substantial improvements, so there’s a clear incentive to keep investing. But extrapolating that trend assumes something about how algorithms, data efficiency, and the cost of computation will evolve. An algorithmic improvement can change those projections quite dramatically.

So I wouldn’t rule out investments on that scale. But I wouldn’t treat a trillion-dollar cluster as an established requirement for more capable AI, either. The interesting question is what additional capability that investment buys you, and whether there are more efficient ways to get there.
